transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-10
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Recording: Fireflies auto
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Carlos Mendes (Redwood SE), Imani Zhou (Redwood), Rajiv Patel (CTO - GreenLedger), Maya Chen (ML Eng), Jordan Lee (Infra), Samir Kahn (PM)

[00:00] Lena Park: hey everyone, thanks for joining, quick check-in on the throughput pilot results from the last 72 hours, how's everyone doing?
[00:08] Rajiv Patel: yep good, thanks. we saw the spikes you warned about, there were a couple windows last night where queue depths climbed, p99 went up to ~650ms from baseline 180ms, so that was concerning.
[00:22] Carlos Mendes: right, we saw the same in the logs — two sustained bursts where concurrency hit the upper limit and batching window stretched, so more prefix batching but also longer wait time per request.
[00:36] Maya Chen: just to add, during the peak we saw KV cache miss rate go up from usual 8% to about 26%, so that blew up per-token work slightly. might be an access pattern thing.
[00:50] Jordan Lee: infra note — our autoscaler did spin up nodes but took about 45s, which is a bit slow for these spikes, and when it happened we had steady backlog building.
[01:03] Imani Zhou: ok, useful. quick question: are you using dedicated capacity or hosted for this pilot? I think you're on the dedicated pool with a small burst envelope?
[01:12] Rajiv Patel: dedicated reserved yes, with a burst cap to hosted we configured but we didn't want traffic going off to hosted unless absolutely necessary.
[01:21] Carlos Mendes: cool, so we have three levers: batching window, per-inference concurrency cap, and a burst/fallback path. suggestion from the last run: reduce the continuous batching window from 60ms to 25-30ms and add a soft concurrency cap per model shard — that reduces tail.
[01:38] Samir Kahn: what do you mean by "soft" cap? will that drop throughput?
[01:41] Carlos Mendes: good question. soft cap means backpressure at router level — we queue up to N concurrent in-flight per model and then let batching absorb. It doesn't drop requests, just increases queuing slightly to keep p99 lower. It's a latency/cost tradeoff.
[01:56] Maya Chen: our success criteria is p99 < 300ms and tokens/sec >= current baseline. if lowering batching window reduces batch efficiency too much we lose tokens/sec.
[02:07] Lena Park: yup that's the core tradeoff. what we saw on the numbers: when we cut window to 30ms in a small test we dropped batch size by ~18% but p99 improved from 650ms to about 260ms under similar load.
[02:21] Rajiv Patel: okay that seems promising. curious about the KV cache priming — can you describe how we should warm the cache for our access pattern?
[02:30] Carlos Mendes: sure. for this workload it's predictable prefixes, so run a background priming job that issues warmup requests with the common prefixes, that brings hit rate up. also we can tune TTL on the cache and the shard mapping. I'll share scripts.
[02:45] Jordan Lee: when you say share scripts where will they live? we prefer S3 with restricted access.
[02:49] Imani Zhou: we'll drop the scripts in the shared drive (S3 link in the notes) and include IAM role info, sample curl and a small python client.
[02:58] Rajiv Patel: related, any reason to move to a smaller quantized variant for burst traffic? lower perf maybe but cheaper and can serve as fallback.
[03:06] Carlos Mendes: exactly — fallback to a q4_qat style variant (example name: rdlw-7b-q4f) during spikes reduces per-token GPU time; the quality drop is small for many system prompts. we can do automatic fallback policy after queue threshold.
[03:20] Maya Chen: we need to test quality drift though; can you run a pass on our validation prompts?
[03:26] Lena Park: yes, we'll run the eval on your prompt set and post the regression report. expect that in the perf spreadsheet.
[03:33] Jordan Lee: ops question: can we get more granular metrics per-shard and per-queue? our current observability is coarse.
[03:40] Carlos Mendes: yes, we can enable per-route histograms and token-level breakdowns in the console, I'll include the config changes.
[03:47] Samir Kahn: timeline wise, what's the recommended next step?
[03:50] Carlos Mendes: propose this: 1) Redwood sends updated config and scripts; 2) GreenLedger runs a 2hr soak during a controlled traffic window with new batching window (25-30ms), concurrency cap (N=48 per shard), and fallback policy enabled; 3) collect p50/p95/p99 and queue depth traces; 4) reconvene.
[04:10] Rajiv Patel: fine by me. question about security — will fallback to smaller quantized variant send any logs externally? we have strict data residency.
[04:19] Lena Park: no, fallback model runs inside the same private pool in your VPC for the dedicated deployment, no data egress to hosted unless you explicitly enable hosted fallback.
[04:28] Jordan Lee: perfect. Also please include the SOC2 artifact link, we need to validate for procurement.
[04:33] Imani Zhou: adding that to the notes.
[04:36] Maya Chen: minor nit: we saw a transient error where tokenization failed for a small subset — looks like a tokenizer mismatch on older model variant.
[04:44] Carlos Mendes: ok we can pin tokenizer versions and add pre-flight checks in the deployment.
[04:48] Lena Park: quick recap and owners — Carlos will send scripts and config; Lena will send spreadsheet; Jordan will run soak and upload logs; Maya will collect latency histograms; Samir will book the follow-up.
[04:59] Rajiv Patel: thanks all.
[05:02] Lena Park: cool — we'll target sendables by Thursday. meeting adjourned.
